title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Euler continues the treatment of quadratic residues modulo an odd prime P = 2n+1 using a primitive root a, whose existence he established earlier in E449.

1. Write the complete residue cycle as 1, a, a^2, ..., a^{2n} ≡ 1, with residues 1, α, β, γ, δ, ε, ζ, η, ..., 1.
2. The squares give residues congruent to the even powers of a: 1, β, δ, ζ, .... Because the sequence a^{2k} repeats with period n, there are exactly n = (P−1)/2 distinct quadratic residues, which is half of the nonzero classes.
3. The odd powers α, γ, ε, η, ... are the n quadratic non-residues. The exception is the divisor 2.
4. Cross-check: the 2n squares 1^2, 2^2, ..., (2n)^2 = 4nn cover all quadratic residues but only n distinct values occur. So the squares must coincide in pairs, and indeed b^2 ≡ (2n+1−b)^2 = (P−b)^2 mod P.
5. Scholion 56 generalizes. The residues of cubes coincide with those of 1, a^3, a^6, .... More generally, the λ-th powers 1, 2^λ, 3^λ, ... mod P give the same set as the powers of a^λ.
6. On the next page Euler concludes the following. If gcd(λ, P−1) = 1, every nonzero class is a λ-th power residue. If gcd(λ, P−1) = d > 1, there are exactly (P−1)/d λ-th power residues.

This material prepares Theorem 57: −1 is a quadratic residue iff n is even, i.e. iff P ≡ 1 mod 4. The argument uses a^n ≡ −1.

In modern terms, Euler is identifying (Z/P)^* with a cyclic group of order P−1 via the index (discrete logarithm). The image of the λ-th power map is then the subgroup generated by a^{gcd(λ,P−1)}, of index d.
errors: No error on this page itself. The whole argument rests on the existence of a primitive root mod P, which E449 attempts to prove earlier. Gauss (Disquisitiones, art. 56) judged Euler's proof incomplete, so the deductions here are only as rigorous as that earlier step.
The phrase 'nisi scilicet binarius pro divisore primo accipiatur' correctly excludes P = 2.

ideas.what: Quadratic residues mod prime P are exactly the even powers of a primitive root; there are (P−1)/2 of them, and the odd powers are the non-residues.
ideas.modern_name: Index characterization of quadratic residues; QR subgroup of index 2 in the cyclic group (Z/P)^*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449, also earlier counting in E242/E262); systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801)
ideas.where_published: E449 (Novi Comment. Acad. Petrop. 18, 1774); counting of residues also in Euler's earlier residue papers (e.g. E262)

ideas.what: b^2 ≡ (P−b)^2, so the squares of 1..P−1 coincide in pairs.
The λ-th power residues mod P coincide with the powers of a^λ, and their number is (P−1)/gcd(λ, P−1).
ideas.modern_name: Image of the λ-th power map in a cyclic group; count of n-th power residues

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard, well-documented content of E449: residues described via indices with respect to a primitive root, and the count of power residues. Gauss explicitly acknowledges this material, and it is covered in standard histories such as Weil's Number Theory. Nothing on the page appears to be new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: Minor notation: the non-residues are printed α, γ, ε, η; the transcription's '\epsilon' should match the 'ε' used on the previous page. No substantive transcription errors found.
